skill.name: Owning or shortening? (its/it's, whose/who's)
skill.why: Mix them up and readers hear 'it is' when you meant owning.
skill.how: Try 'it is', 'it has' or 'who is'. If one fits, use the apostrophe.

steps.say: Zed here! Some words get squashed together.

options.reason: Say it: 'it has snowing again'. Does that sound right?
Nothing is owned here. Say it in full and listen.

steps.win: Yes! It's means 'it is'. A shortening, or contraction.

steps.say: It's can stand for two things. Say it in full.

options.reason: Say it: 'it is been snowing'. Does that sound right?
Nothing is owned here. Say it in full and listen.

steps.win: Yes! It's can mean 'it has' too.

steps.say: Careful! It's looks like owning, but it isn't.
steps.ask: Which word goes with his paw and her paw?

options.reason: It's means 'it is'. Say 'it is paw'. Does that work?
Its' isn't a word. His and her have no apostrophe. Neither does this one.

steps.win: Yes! His, her, its: these never have an apostrophe.

steps.say: Say each one in full: it is, or it has?

show.nudge: Say it in full: 'It is sad.' That works, so it's is right.
Say it in full: 'lost it is hat'? No. This one is owning, like his hat.

steps.ask: One word is wrong. Tap it.
steps.win: Yes! 'It is freezing' works, so it needs it's.

steps.say: Who's and whose work the same way.

show.nudge: Say it in full: 'Who is coming?' That works, so who's is right.
Say it in full: 'Who is hat is this?' No. It asks who owns the hat.

steps.ask: One word is wrong. Tap it.
steps.win: Yes! 'Who is sled' makes no sense. So it's whose.

terms.means: Two words squashed together. It's means it is or it has.
Like his and her. No apostrophe: its, whose.

card.test: Say it in full: it is, it has, who is, who has. Fits? Use the apostrophe.

weDo.hint: Try saying 'it is snowing again'. Does it make sense?
weDo.success: It's. You can say 'it is snowing', so it's a shortening and needs the apostrophe.

options.reason: Its is for owning. Nothing is owned here. It means 'it is snowing'.
An apostrophe after the s shows owners. Is anything owned here? Try saying 'it is'.

weDo.hint: Try saying 'who is beanie is this?'. Does it make sense?
weDo.success: Whose. You're asking who owns the beanie, so it's the owning word with no apostrophe.

options.reason: Who's means 'who is'. 'Who is beanie is this?' makes no sense.
Without an apostrophe this isn't a word. Are you asking 'who is', or who owns it?

creature.name: Dropple
creature.blurb: A snow skink that drops its tail to escape and leaves an apostrophe where the tail was. If nothing is missing, it keeps its tail on.

write.ask: Join these into one sentence. Use it's for one part and its for the other.
given: The yeti has lost the beanie that belongs to it.
checks: My it's still works as 'it is' or 'it has'
My its shows owning and has no apostrophe
write.model: It's freezing tonight, and the yeti has lost its favourite beanie again.

encounters.frame: A snow possum is getting ready to sleep.
encounters.text: The possum curled up in ___ warm nest.
encounters.prompt: Which word fits?
encounters.success: Its. The nest belongs to the possum. Owning its has no apostrophe.

options.reason: It's means 'it is'. 'Curled up in it is warm nest' makes no sense.
An apostrophe after the s shows many owners. One possum owns this nest. Does owning need a mark?

encounters.frame: Tully is shouting from the top of the sled run.
encounters.prompt: Which word fits?
encounters.success: Who's. It means 'who is coming?', so it's a shortening with an apostrophe.

options.reason: Whose asks who owns something. This means 'who is coming?'
'Who is' has been squashed together here. What shows where letters are missing?
